title: Chapter 36 — The Quarter-Deck
paragraphs: (Enter Ahab: Then, all.)

It was not long after the affair of the pipe that one morning shortly after breakfast, Ahab, as usual, climbed the cabin gangway to the deck. There most sea captains usually walk at that hour, the way country gentlemen take a turn in the garden after the same meal.

Soon his steady, ivory stride could be heard as he paced back and forth on his old rounds, over planks so familiar to his step that they were dented all over, like geological stones, with the distinctive marks of his walk. If you stared fixedly at his ribbed and dented brow, you would see still stranger footprints there — the footprints of his one sleepless, ever-pacing thought.

But on this particular occasion, those dents looked deeper, just as his nervous step that morning left a deeper mark. Ahab was so full of his thought that at every regular turn he made — now at the mainmast, now at the binnacle — you could almost see that thought turn inside him as he turned, and pace inside him as he paced. It possessed him so completely, in fact, that it all but seemed the inner mold of every outward movement.
"Do you notice him, Flask?" whispered Stubb. "The chick inside him is pecking at the shell. It'll be out soon."
The hours wore on — Ahab now shut up in his cabin, then pacing the deck again, with the same intense, fanatical purpose in his face.
The day was drawing to a close. Suddenly he stopped by the bulwarks, inserted his bone leg into the auger-hole there, and with one hand gripping a shroud, he ordered Starbuck to send everyone aft.
"Sir!" said the mate, astonished at an order seldom or never given on a ship except in some extraordinary situation.
"Send everybody aft," repeated Ahab. "Mastheads, there! Come down!"

When the entire ship's company was assembled and, with curious and somewhat uneasy faces, was watching him — for he looked not unlike the windward horizon when a storm is coming up — Ahab, after glancing quickly over the bulwarks and then darting his eyes among the crew, left his post. As though no one were near him, he resumed his heavy pacing across the deck. With bent head and half-slouched hat, he continued to pace, ignoring the wondering whispers among the men, until Stubb cautiously whispered to Flask that Ahab must have assembled them to witness some kind of walking performance. But this didn't last long. Pausing forcefully, he cried:
"What do you do when you see a whale, men?"
"Sing out for him!" was the instant answer from a score of voices in unison.
"Good!" cried Ahab, wild approval in his voice, as he watched the hearty excitement his unexpected question had so magnetically stirred in them.
"And what do you do next, men?"
"Lower away, and after him!"
"And what tune do you pull to, men?"
"A dead whale or a stove boat!"

Stranger and fiercer grew the glad, approving look on the old man's face with every shout. Meanwhile, the sailors began glancing curiously at each other, as if marveling at how they themselves had become so excited by such seemingly pointless questions.
But they were all eagerness again as Ahab, now half-revolving in his pivot-hole, one hand reaching high up a shroud and gripping it tightly, almost convulsively, addressed them:

"All you masthead-standers have already heard me give orders about a white whale. Look here! Do you see this Spanish gold ounce?" — holding up a broad, bright coin to the sun — "It's a sixteen-dollar piece, men. Do you see it? Mr. Starbuck, hand me that top-maul."

While the mate went for the hammer, Ahab, without speaking, slowly rubbed the gold piece against the skirts of his jacket, as if to heighten its shine. Without using any words, he hummed softly to himself, making a sound so strangely muffled and unclear that it seemed like the mechanical humming of the wheels of his vitality inside him.

Taking the top-maul from Starbuck, he advanced toward the mainmast with the hammer raised in one hand and the gold coin displayed in the other, and in a loud, raised voice he cried: "Whichever of you spots me a white-headed whale with a wrinkled brow and a crooked jaw — whichever of you spots me that white-headed whale with three holes punctured in his starboard fluke — look here, whichever of you spots me that same white whale, he shall have this gold ounce, my boys!"
"Hurrah! Hurrah!" cried the seamen, swinging their tarpaulin hats as they cheered the act of nailing the gold to the mast.
"It's a white whale, I say," Ahab continued, throwing down the hammer. "A white whale. Keep your eyes peeled for him, men. Watch for white water. If you see so much as a bubble, sing out."

All this time, Tashtego, Daggoo, and Queequeg had been watching with even more intense interest and surprise than the rest. At the mention of the wrinkled brow and crooked jaw, they had each started as if individually touched by some specific memory.
"Captain Ahab," said Tashtego, "that white whale must be the same one some call Moby Dick."
"Moby Dick?" shouted Ahab. "Do you know the white whale, then, Tash?"
"Does he spread his tail a little strangely, sir, before he dives?" said the Gay Header deliberately.
"And does he have an unusual spout, too," said Daggoo, "very bushy, even for a sperm whale, and very quick, Captain Ahab?"

"And he have one, two, three — oh! many many iron in him hide, too, Captain," cried Queequeg in his broken way, "all twiske-tee be-twisk, like him — him —" struggling for the word and screwing his hand round and round as if uncorking a bottle — "like him — him —"

"Corkscrew!" cried Ahab. "Yes, Queequeg, the harpoons lie all twisted and wrenched in him. Yes, Daggoo, his spout is a big one, like a whole sheaf of wheat, and white as a pile of our Nantucket wool after the great annual sheep-shearing. Yes, Tashtego, and he fans his tail like a split jib in a squall. Death and devils! Men, it is Moby Dick you have seen — Moby Dick — Moby Dick!"

"Captain Ahab," said Starbuck, who with Stubb and Flask had been watching his superior with growing surprise but now seemed struck by a thought that somewhat explained the wonder, "Captain Ahab, I have heard of Moby Dick — but it was not Moby Dick that took off your leg?"

"Who told you that?" cried Ahab. Then, pausing: "Yes, Starbuck. Yes, my hearties, all of you. It was Moby Dick that dismasted me. Moby Dick that brought me to this dead stump I stand on now. Yes, yes!" he shouted with a terrible, loud, animal sob, like that of a heart-stricken moose. "Yes, yes! It was that accursed white whale that razeed me — cut me down like a warship sheared of its upper deck — and made a poor peg-legged lubber of me forever and a day!" Then, throwing both arms wide, with measureless curses he shouted: "Yes, yes! And I'll chase him around the Cape of Good Hope, and around the Horn, and around the Norway Maelstrom, and around the flames of hell before I give him up. And this is what you have signed on for, men! To chase that white whale on both sides of land, and over all sides of earth, until he spouts black blood and rolls fin out. What do you say, men — will you splice hands on it now? I think you look brave."
"Yes! Yes!" shouted the harpooners and seamen, running closer to the excited old man. "A sharp eye for the white whale! A sharp lance for Moby Dick!"

"God bless you," he seemed to half sob and half shout. "God bless you, men. Steward! Go draw the great measure of grog. But what's this long face about, Mr. Starbuck? Won't you chase the white whale? Aren't you game for Moby Dick?"

"I'll face his crooked jaw, and the jaws of Death too, Captain Ahab, if it fairly comes in the way of the business we're here for. But I came here to hunt whales, not my commander's vengeance. How many barrels will your vengeance yield you, even if you get it, Captain Ahab? It won't fetch you much in our Nantucket market."

"Nantucket market! Ha! But come closer, Starbuck — you need to go a layer deeper. If money is to be the measure, man, and the accountants have computed their great counting-house, the globe, by girdling it with guineas, one to every three parts of an inch — then let me tell you that my vengeance will fetch a great premium here!"
"He strikes his chest," whispered Stubb. "What's that for? It seems to ring vast, but hollow."
"Vengeance on a dumb animal!" cried Starbuck. "That simply struck you from blindest instinct! Madness! To be enraged with a mindless creature, Captain Ahab, seems blasphemous."

"Listen again — the deeper layer. All visible things, man, are nothing but cardboard masks. But in each event — in the living act, the undeniable deed — there, some unknown but still reasoning thing puts forth the molded shape of its features from behind the unreasoning mask. If a man would strike, strike through the mask! How can the prisoner reach outside except by thrusting through the wall? To me, the white whale is that wall, shoved close against me. Sometimes I think there's nothing beyond it. But that's enough. He tasks me. He heaps me. I see in him outrageous strength, with an inscrutable malice giving it sinew. That inscrutable thing is chiefly what I hate. And whether the white whale is the agent or the principal, I will wreak that hate upon him. Don't talk to me of blasphemy, man — I'd strike the sun if it insulted me. For if the sun could do that, then I could do the other, since there is always a kind of fair play in this, with jealousy presiding over all creation. But not even that fair play is my master, man. Who is over me? Truth knows no boundaries. Take your eyes off me! More unbearable than a fiend's glare is a dull, stupid stare! So, so — you flush red and go pale. My heat has melted you into an angry glow. But listen, Starbuck — what is said in heat unsays itself. There are men from whom hot words are only a small indignity. I didn't mean to provoke you. Let it go. Look! See those Turkish cheeks of spotted tawny brown — living, breathing pictures painted by the sun. The pagan leopards — the heedless, unworshipping things that live and seek and give no reasons for the torrid life they feel! The crew, man, the crew! Aren't they one and all with Ahab in this matter of the whale? See Stubb — he laughs! See that Chilean — he snorts just thinking of it. Stand up against the general hurricane? Your one tossed sapling cannot, Starbuck! And what is it? Think about it. It's only helping to strike a fin — no great feat for Starbuck. What more is it? From this one poor hunt, then, the best lance out of all Nantucket will surely not hang back, when every common sailor has already grabbed a whetstone? Ah! Compulsions seize you — I see it! The wave lifts you! Speak — speak! Yes, yes! Your silence, then — that speaks for you. (Aside) Something shot from my flaring nostrils, and he has breathed it into his lungs. Starbuck is mine now. He cannot oppose me now without rebellion."
"God keep me! — keep us all!" murmured Starbuck, quietly.

But in his joy at the mate's enchanted, silent consent, Ahab did not hear his ominous prayer. Nor the low laugh from the hold. Nor the foreboding vibrations of the wind in the rigging. Nor the hollow flap of the sails against the masts, as for a moment their hearts sank in. For again Starbuck's downcast eyes lit up with the stubbornness of life. The subterranean laugh died away. The winds blew on. The sails filled out. The ship heaved and rolled as before. Ah, you warnings and omens! Why don't you stay when you come? But rather than warnings, you are predictions — you shadows! Yet not so much predictions from outside as confirmations of what was already inside. For with little to restrain us from without, the deepest necessities within our being still drive us on.
"The measure! The measure!" cried Ahab.

Receiving the brimming pewter mug and turning to the harpooners, he ordered them to produce their weapons. Then, lining them up before him near the capstan with their harpoons in hand, while his three mates stood at his side with their lances and the rest of the crew formed a circle around the group, he stood for a moment searching every man's face. Those wild eyes met his the way the bloodshot eyes of prairie wolves meet the eye of their leader before he rushes ahead of the pack on the trail of the buffalo — but alas, only to fall into the hidden trap of the Indian.

"Drink and pass!" he cried, handing the heavy, full flagon to the nearest seaman. "The crew alone drinks now. Pass it round! Short sips — long swallows, men. It's hot as Satan's hoof. Good, good — it goes round well. It spirals into you. It forks out at the serpent-snapping eye. Well done — nearly drained. That way it went, this way it comes. Hand it back — here's a hollow! Men, you are like the years: brimming life is gulped and gone. Steward, refill!"

"Listen now, my brave ones. I have gathered you all around this capstan. You mates, flank me with your lances. You harpooners, stand there with your irons. And you, stout sailors, ring me in, so I may in some fashion revive a noble custom of my fisherman fathers before me. O men, you will yet see that — Ha! Boy, back already? Bad pennies don't come back any sooner. Hand it here. Why, now, this pewter would have run brimming again if you weren't such a St. Vitus' imp — away with you, you shaking fever!"

"Advance, you mates! Cross your lances before me. Good! Let me touch the center." So saying, with extended arm he grasped the three level, radiating lances at their crossed center point. As he did so, he suddenly and nervously twitched them, meanwhile looking intently from Starbuck to Stubb, from Stubb to Flask. It seemed as though by some nameless, inner force of will, he wanted to shock into them the same fiery emotion stored in the Leyden jar of his own magnetic life. The three mates quailed before his strong, sustained, mystic presence. Stubb and Flask looked sideways away from him. The honest eye of Starbuck fell straight to the deck.

"In vain!" cried Ahab. "But maybe that's for the best. For if you three had once taken the full-forced shock, then my own electric thing might perhaps have drained out of me. Perhaps, too, it would have dropped you dead. Perhaps you don't need it. Lower lances! And now, you mates, I appoint you three cupbearers to my three pagan kinsmen there — those three most honorable gentlemen and noblemen, my valiant harpooners. You disdain the task? What — when the great Pope washes the feet of beggars, using his tiara for a water jug? Oh, my sweet cardinals! Your own condescension — that will bend you to it. I don't command you — you will it. Cut your lashings and draw the poles, you harpooners!"
Silently obeying the order, the three harpooners now stood holding the detached iron tips of their harpoons, about three feet long, barbs pointing up, before him.

"Don't stab me with that sharp steel! Tilt them — tilt them over! Don't you know the goblet end? Turn up the socket! Good, good. Now, you cupbearers, step forward. The irons! Take them. Hold them while I fill!" Then, slowly going from one officer to the next, he filled the harpoon sockets to the brim with the fiery liquor from the pewter.

"Now, three to three, you stand. Present the murderous chalices! Hand them over, you who are now partners in this unbreakable league. Ha! Starbuck! — but the deed is done! That ratifying sun now waits to set its seal on it. Drink, you harpooners! Drink and swear, you men who man the deadly whaleboat's bow — Death to Moby Dick! God hunt us all if we do not hunt Moby Dick to his death!" The long, barbed steel goblets were raised. To cries and curses against the white whale, the spirits were gulped down together with a hiss. Starbuck paled, turned, and shuddered. Once more, and finally, the refilled pewter went the rounds among the frenzied crew. Then, as he waved his free hand to them, they all dispersed, and Ahab retired to his cabin.
